terms.definition: A triangle with three acute angles.
A triangle with one right angle.
A triangle with one obtuse angle.
A triangle with no congruent sides.
A triangle with at least two congruent sides.
A triangle with three congruent sides.
An angle formed by one side of a triangle and the extension of an adjacent side.
The two interior angles not adjacent to a chosen exterior angle.
The matching of vertices, sides, and angles between two figures.
Triangles with the same size and shape; all corresponding sides and angles are congruent.
A triangle congruence criterion using three corresponding side pairs.
A triangle congruence criterion using two corresponding side pairs and their included angle.
A triangle congruence criterion using two corresponding angle pairs and the included side.
A triangle congruence criterion using two corresponding angle pairs and a non-included side.
A right-triangle congruence criterion using congruent hypotenuses and one pair of congruent legs.
The angle between two specified sides.
The side between two specified angles.
The side opposite the right angle in a right triangle.
Either side forming the right angle in a right triangle.
Three angle correspondences; sufficient for similarity but not triangle congruence.
Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent; used after triangle congruence is established.
A geometric object is congruent to itself.
For a nondegenerate triangle, the sum of any two side lengths is greater than the third.
A boundary case in which three points are collinear and one side length equals the sum of the other two.
A line perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint; its points are equidistant from the segment endpoints.
A ray or segment that divides an angle into two congruent angles.
A segment from a triangle vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
A perpendicular segment from a triangle vertex to the line containing the opposite side.
The intersection of the perpendicular bisectors; equidistant from the triangle's vertices.
The intersection of the angle bisectors; equidistant from the triangle's sides.
The intersection of the medians; divides each median in a 2:1 ratio from vertex to midpoint.
The intersection of the triangle's altitudes.
The property of three or more lines meeting at one point.
